extra.message: Insecure Deserialization via pickle.loads on attacker-controlled input — Remote code execution on the server if the attacker obtains or bypasses the internal ops token [verified: Same as finding 1: attacker-controlled bytes deserialized by `pickle.loads()` at line 70 with no input sanitization.]

OS Command Injection via unsanitized shell command construction — Arbitrary shell command execution on the server with the application's privileges [verified: Same as finding 0: `host` GET param directly interpolated into shell command via `os.system()` at line 133 with no escaping.]

OS command injection via ping in case_shell_probe_502 — Remote code execution on the server as the Django process user; full filesystem access, data exfiltration, lateral movement. [verified: Same as finding 0: `host` GET param flows unsanitized into `os.system("ping -c 1 " + host)` at line 133, enabling shell command injection past the `_wrk_gate` token check.]

Weak default SECRET_KEY in settings — Session forgery, CSRF token forgery, password reset token forgery — full account takeover of any user. [verified: Same weak SECRET_KEY default 'dev-only-change-me'; no compensating control exists — if the env var is missing, every session cookie, CSRF token, and password-reset token is signed with this known key, enabling forgery and full account takeover.]

Hardcoded weak default Django SECRET_KEY — Session forgery, CSRF token bypass, and password reset token forgery if the default key is used in any environment [verified: Same weak SECRET_KEY default 'dev-only-change-me'; no production guard or mandatory override exists, so any instance missing DJANGO_SECRET_KEY in its environment uses this known key for all cryptographic signing, enabling session/CSRF/password-reset token forgery.]

Missing rate limiting on authentication endpoints — Credential brute-forcing, account enumeration, and denial of service via password-reset email flooding. [verified: No rate limiting exists on /login/, /register/, or /password-reset/ — requirements.txt contains only Django, psycopg2-binary, and python-dotenv with no django-ratelimit, django-axes, or custom throttle decorators, and no middleware implements brute-force protection; Django has no built-in rate limiting.]

Path Traversal via uploaded filename in ops file storage — Arbitrary file write on the server filesystem under the storage location, potential for code execution or data corruption. [verified: `drop_blob.name` (line 33) is the original attacker-supplied upload filename passed directly to `shelf.save()` or `packet_ref` GET param (line 36) is used as the storage path; no path sanitization is performed, enabling writes outside the intended `private_exports/incoming` directory.]

Code Injection via unsafe eval() with user-controlled expression — Arbitrary Python code execution on the server if the attacker knows the internal ops token [verified: Same as finding 2: `expr` GET param evaluated by `eval()` at line 81 with restricted builtins bypassable via object introspection.]

Path Traversal arbitrary file write via unsanitized filename parameter — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem, leading to code execution or system compromise [verified: Same as finding 5: unsanitized `name` GET param used as file path for `write_bytes()` at line 134, enabling arbitrary filesystem writes.]

Path traversal / arbitrary file write in case_dock_shelf_499 — Arbitrary file write anywhere on the filesystem reachable by the Django process; could plant cron jobs, overwrite application code, drop webshells. [verified: Same as finding 5: `name` GET param joined to `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` then `write_bytes()` at line 134 with no path sanitization, enabling arbitrary file write.]

XXE via lxml parser with DTD and entity resolution enabled — Local file disclosure, server-side request forgery, and potential denial of service [verified: Same as finding 3: `lxml.etree.XMLParser(resolve_entities=True, load_dtd=True, no_network=False)` at line 157 enables XXE on attacker-supplied XML.]

NoSQL Injection via user-controlled MongoDB query filter — JavaScript execution on the MongoDB server, data exfiltration, or denial of service [verified: Same as finding 4: JSON body parsed and used as unsanitized MongoDB `find_one()` query at line 178.]

XXE via lxml etree with resolve_entities enabled — Arbitrary local file read (SECRET_KEY, database credentials, source code) and internal SSRF from the server. [verified: XML from `request.body` is parsed at line 158 via `lxml.etree.XMLParser(load_dtd=True, resolve_entities=True, no_network=False)`, which explicitly enables external entity resolution; this allows XXE-based local file read and SSRF through crafted XML entities.]

NoSQL Injection via unsanitized MongoDB query — Bypass MongoDB query filters, read arbitrary documents, potential server-side JavaScript execution, denial of service. [verified: JSON body is parsed and `payload.get("filter", payload)` at line 177 is passed directly as a MongoDB query to `find_one()` with no sanitization, allowing injection of operators like `$where` or `$regex` into the query.]

Missing Rate Limiting on authentication endpoints — Credential brute-forcing, account takeover, and denial of service against login/register/reset endpoints [verified: No rate limiting (django-axes, custom throttle, or decorator) is present on /login/, /register/, or /password-reset/; Django has no built-in brute-force protection, and no compensating control was found in middleware, views, or dependencies, leaving credentials and reset tokens open to unlimited guessing.]

DEBUG mode enabled by default in production — Full information disclosure: stack traces, SECRET_KEY exposure, database credentials, internal paths, and unauthenticated access to uploaded media files. [verified: Same DEBUG=True default — the .env.example also sets DJANGO_DEBUG=1; detailed error pages expose SECRET_KEY, database credentials, internal paths, and SQL queries, while urls.py:10-11 serves uploaded media without auth, making all confidential files publicly accessible.]

DEBUG=True by default exposes sensitive information — Disclosure of stack traces, file paths, database queries, and configuration secrets to any unauthenticated user who triggers an error. [verified: DEBUG defaults to True via os.getenv('DJANGO_DEBUG','1')=='1'; when enabled, Django's error pages leak stack traces, local variables, SECRET_KEY, DB credentials, and SQL queries to any unauthenticated user who triggers an error, and urls.py:10-11 serves media files without authentication.]

Plaintext API key storage in database — Database compromise exposes all API keys in usable form, enabling impersonation of any API key holder and unauthorized access to matter status data via the API endpoint. [verified: ApiKey.key is a plaintext CharField (line 264) stored as-is via secrets.token_urlsafe; api_matter_status (line 565) queries by raw key value with no hashing. No pre_save/post_save signals or make_password calls exist anywhere in the codebase to hash keys before storage, so a database compromise exposes all usable API keys.]

Business logic bypass: matter_edit allows unvalidated status transitions skipping ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS workflow — An attorney or paralegal with legitimate edit access to a matter can skip mandated workflow stages (e.g., jump from INTAKE directly to ARCHIVED, bypassing CONFLICT_REVIEW, OPEN, and CLOSED), undermining process controls and audit trail integrity. Could be used to prematurely archive or close matters to hide them from normal workflow views. [verified: MatterForm includes 'status' in Meta.fields (forms.py line 57) and its clean() only validates closed_date presence — it does NOT validate transition legality; the matter_edit view (views.py line 172) calls form.save() which invokes Django's default ModelForm.save() → Model.save(), completely bypassing Matter.transition_to() which enforces ALLOWED_TRANSITIONS (models.py lines 88-94).]

Missing Authorization scope check allowing cross-client data access in client_edit — Attorneys and paralegals can view and modify any client's data regardless of matter assignment [verified: client_edit only checks request.user.role in {FIRM_ADMIN, ATTORNEY, PARALEGAL} (line 210) then fetches any Client by pk with get_object_or_404; authz.py has no can_access_client function and client_list already exposes all clients to any staff member — no matter-assignment or client-scoping check exists for attorneys/paralegals, allowing cross-client data access.]

CSV Formula Injection in export via unsanitized user-controlled cell values — Arbitrary command execution on the victim's machine when exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software [verified: Same CSV injection sink as finding 0 — export_csv writes unsanitized database values (seeded via ImportForm which stores raw CSV without formula sanitization at lines 475-495) directly to csv.writer output; no sanitization exists for =, +, -, @ cell prefixes.]

CSV Formula Injection in export endpoints — When exported CSV is opened in spreadsheet software, attacker-controlled formulas execute arbitrary commands or exfiltrate data from the analyst's machine. [verified: export_csv writes database fields (matter titles, client names, document titles) directly to CSV via csv.writer with no sanitization of formula-triggering prefixes (=, +, -, @); data arrives unsanitized from ImportForm.rows() (line 475-495) which passes raw CSV values to update_or_create, and no sanitization layer exists anywhere between input and export sink.]

API key exposed in HTML flash message in integrations view — API key leakage through browser history, page caching, or DOM inspection; enables unauthorized API access. [verified: The integrations view (line 549) passes the plaintext API key via messages.success() rendered as {{ message }} in base.html; the key appears in the HTML page source and persists in browser history/cache for that page render, with no one-time-only modal or removal mechanism.]

Missing Authentication on internal operations endpoint exposing sensitive data — Unauthenticated access to internal operational intelligence data [verified: Same as finding 8: `case_matter_file_048` lacks `_wrk_gate()` and returns sensitive operational data unauthenticated.]

Sensitive Data Exposure via logging of request body and Authorization header — Exposure of credentials, tokens, or sensitive data to anyone with log access [verified: Same as finding 12: request body and Authorization header logged in plaintext at line 73 via `logger.warning()`.]

Log injection and sensitive token exposure in case_wire_tally_217 — Log forgery (inject fake log entries via CRLF in body); exposure of INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN or other credentials in log files, enabling an attacker who reads logs to bypass the ops gate entirely. [verified: Same as finding 12: full request body and Authorization header logged at WARNING level at line 73 with no redaction.]

Permissive CORS configuration echoing arbitrary Origin with credentials — Cross-origin attacks from any domain with user credentials, enabling data theft and CSRF-like attacks [verified: Same as finding 7: `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` echoes arbitrary `Origin` header with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.]

Weak PRNG — random.choice instead of secrets for token generation in ops nonce endpoint — An attacker who can observe multiple nonce outputs can predict future tokens, compromising any security use of those tokens (session identifiers, CSRF tokens, password reset tokens). [verified: case_nonce_roll_511 uses random.choice() (Mersenne Twister, not cryptographically secure) with a user-controlled 'length' parameter to generate tokens; the endpoint is reachable behind the ops token gate and no secrets module or CSPRNG is used.]

Password reset tokens written to plaintext files via file-based email backend — Password reset tokens and other sensitive emails readable by anyone with filesystem access; enables account takeover. [verified: EMAIL_BACKEND is filebased.EmailBackend writing to var/mail/; password-reset emails (containing single-use account-takeover tokens) are stored as plaintext files — anyone with filesystem read access to that directory can extract tokens and compromise accounts.]

User enumeration via registration form error messages — Attackers can build a list of valid usernames for targeted credential-stuffing or phishing attacks. [verified: RegistrationForm inherits Django's UserCreationForm which validates unique usernames and returns 'A user with that username already exists.' on duplicates; no custom clean_username override masks this, allowing unauthenticated attackers to enumerate valid accounts via form error differentiation.]

Account Enumeration via registration form username uniqueness error — Enumeration of valid user accounts enabling targeted credential attacks [verified: Identical to finding 2 — Django's UserCreationForm unique-username validation produces distinguishable error messages on /register/, enabling unauthenticated username enumeration with no custom masking.]

Open Redirect via unvalidated redirect target parameter — Phishing attacks by redirecting users to attacker-controlled domains [verified: Same as finding 9: user-controlled `lane` parameter passed to `redirect()` at line 58 with no validation.]

Missing cookie security flags — no Secure/HttpOnly/SameSite on portal_crumb cookie — Cookie value is vulnerable to theft via MITM on HTTP connections, exfiltration via XSS, and inclusion in cross-site requests enabling CSRF-style attacks. [verified: case_crumb_lane_295 sets the 'portal_crumb' cookie via response.set_cookie() with no Secure, HttpOnly, or SameSite flags; the cookie value is user-controlled via the 'marker' GET parameter and no compensating cookie configuration is applied.]

Internal path disclosure in error response via case_pulse_spill_348 — Reconnaissance — attacker learns the server's internal directory layout (`/path/to/app/private_exports`), which aids in path traversal and other filesystem attacks. [verified: Same as finding 14: `RuntimeError` at line 100 includes `BASE_EXPORT_DIR` path, returned to client via `str(exc)` at line 102.]

Hardcoded credentials — verifier PINs embedded in ops identity endpoint source — Secondary authentication in the ops identity endpoint is bypassable by anyone who obtains the source code, allowing unauthorized access to the 'queued' status response. [verified: case_identity_hint_461 hardcodes verifier PINs {'north':'4812','south':'5930'} directly in source; though gated behind the ops token, anyone with source access can trivially bypass the secondary verifier check.]

SSL/TLS Certificate Verification Disabled for outbound HTTPS requests — Man-in-the-middle attacks intercepting or modifying outbound HTTPS traffic [verified: Same as finding 11: `ssl._create_unverified_context()` used for outbound HTTPS with no peer certificate verification.]

TLS certificate verification disabled for outbound HTTPS — Man-in-the-middle attacks on outbound HTTPS connections, allowing interception and modification of data sent to partner endpoints. [verified: `ssl._create_unverified_context()` at line 188 disables TLS certificate verification for the outbound HTTPS request; although the hardcoded target `partner.invalid` uses a reserved TLD that never resolves, the insecure SSL context is genuinely present on a reachable code path.]
